title: How long, O Lord? (Psalm 13)
hook: the Bible gives you permission to complain to God

segments.voice: Yesterday, intercession, and your line: hold them up. Whose name did you carry? This week, ways to pray: the Jesus Prayer, the Psalms, lectio divina, the examen, arrows, names. Today, the one people are surprised is allowed. Day one hundred five.

It's two in the morning. The diagnosis hasn't changed. The job still hasn't come through. The person still hasn't called back. You've been polite about it for months. And somewhere inside, a very impolite question is building. Many people assume there are two options here: swallow it, or walk away from God entirely. The Bible offers a third, and it's in the middle of its own prayer book. A psalm that opens with a complaint, and doesn't apologize for it. In the King James words: "How long wilt thou forget me, O LORD? for ever? how long wilt thou hide thy face from me?" That's not a whisper. That's somebody at the end of their rope, talking straight to God. Today's word is what this kind of prayer is called.
screen: `TWO IN THE MORNING.` → `SWALLOW IT, OR WALK AWAY?` → `A THIRD WAY: HOW LONG?`

segments.voice: Lament. A prayer of grief and complaint, spoken to God. You met this psalm back on day seventeen, with David shouting at God. Today, look at how a lament is built, because the shape is the teaching. The first two verses ask how long, four times. Then the psalm asks for something: "Consider and hear me, O LORD my God: lighten mine eyes." Look at me. Answer me. And then it turns: "But I have trusted in thy mercy; my heart shall rejoice in thy salvation." Complaint, request, trust. Notice what hasn't changed. Nothing outside. No answer arrives between verse four and verse five. The turn happens in the one praying. Scholars count around a third of the Psalms as laments, and some aren't one person's cry but a whole people's, after a defeat or a famine. Not all of them turn; Psalm 88 never does. Then there's a whole book of lament. Lamentations grieves Jerusalem after the Babylonians burned it. And look at how it's made. Four of its five chapters are acrostics: each verse starts with the next letter of the Hebrew alphabet. Grief, set out from A to Z. Some readers hear in that a way of saying all of it, every letter, and of giving pain a shape with an end. Here's the idea under all of it. You don't complain to someone you think isn't there. A lament keeps talking to God while saying, this hurts, and it isn't right. Jews have prayed these psalms for many centuries, and on Tisha B'Av, the fast that mourns the temple, Lamentations is chanted aloud. Christians of every church pray the laments too. For both, honesty isn't the opposite of faith. Sometimes it's what faith sounds like at two in the morning.
screen: `HOW LONG? FOUR TIMES.` · `COMPLAINT, REQUEST, TRUST.` · `GRIEF FROM A TO Z.` · then, large: `YOU DON'T COMPLAIN TO NOBODY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: write one honest complaint. Get something to write on, or open a note on your phone. Settle, and breathe. What's the thing you've been polite about for too long? Write it in one or two sentences, plainly. If you pray, you can start it the way the psalm does: how long. If you don't pray, write it to whoever or whatever you'd want to hear it. Don't tidy it up. Don't add a happy ending unless one comes. Then put the pen down and sit with it. The bell holds the time.
Lament. A prayer of grief and complaint, spoken to God rather than about him. Around a third of the Psalms are laments. Today's word.
Your line: complaint is a prayer too. Today, keep what you wrote. Read it once more tonight, and notice whether anything has shifted, even a little. Fifteen weeks on the path. Day one hundred five.

howItsDone: Christians pray the lament psalms in daily prayer, at funerals and in times of crisis, and many churches hold services of lament after tragedies; some people write their own complaints to God in a journal, following the psalms' shape.

original.note: Hebrew: how long? the words that open Psalm 13's complaint, again and again.

trapdoor: what you thought: you're not supposed to complain to God.
what it means: the Bible's own prayer book is full of complaint. Psalm 13 asks how long four times before it turns to trust.
what a scholar hears: Lamentations 1–4 are acrostics, each verse opening with the next Hebrew letter; chapter 3 gives every letter three verses.

notes: 'Around a third' of the Psalms as laments (individual and communal) follows common scholarly counts (e.g. in form criticism after Gunkel); counts vary by method. Confirm the phrasing.
Psalm 13 is six verses in English; in Hebrew the superscription makes it verses 1–6 with numbering offset. Screen head 'HOW LONG? FOUR TIMES' refers to verses 1–2 in the KJV.
Psalm 88 described as ending in darkness with no turn: the standard reading. Confirm.
